summary.text: Biochemistry is the study of chemical processes within and relating to living organisms.
It is a sub-discipline of both chemistry and biology and may be divided into structural biology, enzymology, and metabolism.
Its findings are applied mainly in medicine, nutrition, and agriculture, and combined with engineering methods it gives biotechnology.

paragraphs.heading: The chemistry of life
paragraphs.text: Biochemistry, also called biological chemistry, studies the chemical processes that go on inside living things and are linked to them. It belongs to both chemistry and biology. It tries to understand the chemistry that lets biological molecules produce what happens inside cells and between them, which in turn helps explain tissues, organs and the build and working of whole organisms. It has close ties to molecular biology, which studies the molecular mechanisms behind biological events.

paragraphs.heading: Three main fields
paragraphs.text: The subject can be split into three fields: structural biology, enzymology and metabolism. Metabolism means the ways cells capture energy from their surroundings through chemical reactions. Much of the work concerns proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates, lipids and other biological macromolecules, looking at their structures, roles and interactions. These molecules make up the structure of cells and carry out many of the jobs that go with being alive. In the closing decades of the 20th century, the three fields became good at explaining living processes.

paragraphs.heading: Small molecules and elements
paragraphs.text: Cell chemistry also relies on small molecules and ions. Some are inorganic, like water and metal ions; others are organic, like the amino acids that cells use to build proteins. Around two dozen chemical elements are essential to one form of life or another. Just six, known as CHNOPS: carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus and sulfur, make up more than 99% of the mass of our cells. Humans also need large amounts of four ions, magnesium, potassium, sodium and calcium, and small amounts of others called micronutrients.

paragraphs.heading: What it is used for
paragraphs.text: The findings of biochemistry are put to use mainly in medicine, nutrition and agriculture. In medicine, biochemists look into what causes diseases and how to cure them. Nutrition asks how to stay healthy and what happens when the diet falls short. In farming, biochemists study soil and fertilizers to improve how crops are grown and stored and how pests are controlled. Combined with engineering methods to change living systems, biochemistry becomes biotechnology, which yields tools for research, industry and the diagnosis and control of disease.

paragraphs.heading: When did it begin
paragraphs.text: As a separate science, biochemistry began in the 19th century or slightly before, with the date depending on which part of it you look at. Some date its start to 1833, when Anselme Payen found the first enzyme, diastase, now called amylase. Others choose 1897, when Eduard Buchner showed alcoholic fermentation happening in extracts with no cells. Still others point to Justus von Liebig's 1842 work Animal chemistry, or back to Antoine Lavoisier's 18th-century studies of fermentation and respiration. The word first appeared in print in 1858, in Vinzenz Kletzinsky's Compendium der Biochemie, printed in Vienna.

paragraphs.heading: Beyond the vital spark
paragraphs.text: People once widely believed that living things held a special 'vital principle' found nowhere in non-living matter, and that only living beings could make the molecules of life. In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler published his accidental synthesis of urea from potassium cyanate and ammonium sulfate. Some saw it as overthrowing vitalism, though others reject that view. Since the mid-20th century, methods such as chromatography, X-ray diffraction, NMR spectroscopy and electron microscopy have uncovered many of the cell's molecules and pathways, including glycolysis and the Krebs cycle.
